title.en: Hervor and Tyrfing: The Shieldmaiden Who Woke the Dead for a Sword
title.zh: 赫爾沃與提爾芬：為奪劍而喚醒亡者的女戰士

region.en: The mound of Angantyr on Samsø, Denmark
region.zh: 丹麥薩姆索島上的安甘提爾之墓

texts.period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (older heroic material; verse Hervararkvida of older date); principal MS Hauksbok AM 544 4to; English: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, 1921

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Hervararkvida); ed. C. C. Rafn, Fornaldar sogur; English trans. Nora Kershaw 1921; trans. Christopher Tolkien 1960

texts.license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hervor is the daughter of Angantyr, the berserk who died with his eleven brothers on the island of Samsø, buried in a mound with the cursed sword Tyrfing. Raised as a bondmaid in her mother's house, she learns her father's name, dresses as a man, and takes ship to the haunted island. Alone at night she walks the burning fire of the grave-mounds and calls the dead: 'Wake, Angantyr! Hervor wakes you, only daughter of Yngvi's kin!' The dead warn her; father Angantyr tells her the sword burns its holders; she persists, and the mound opens, and she takes Tyrfing from the dead man's hand - the only person to claim a cursed weapon from its own corpse. The record is the fornaldarsaga's signature descent: a living woman entering the world of the dead by command-voice, and winning its treasure against its own warning.
summary.zh: 赫爾沃是狂戰士安甘提爾之女——他與十一位兄弟死於薩姆索島，連同詛咒之劍提爾芬一同葬於墳丘。赫爾沃在母親家中被當作奴婢養大，得知父親之名後即改著男裝，乘船前往那座鬧鬼之島。夜深人靜，她獨自穿越墳墓間的鬼火，高聲呼喚亡者：「醒來吧，安甘提爾！喚你的是赫爾沃，英格維一族的獨女！」亡者出言警告；父親安甘提爾更告訴她，此劍必將反噬其主。她毫不退縮；墳丘終於開啟，她自死人手中取走提爾芬——唯一敢從詛咒武器的屍主手中將其奪走的人。此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》的代表性冥府之行：一名生者女子以號令之聲踏入亡者世界，無視其警告，贏得其中寶物。

texts.canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain); Christopher Tolkien, The Saga of King Heidrek the Wise, 1960

narrative.en:
The saga's first movement is Hervor's doubling. Her father Angantyr, berserk of the Arngrim-lineage? - of Arngrim's sons, died on Samsø in the berserk-duel with the Jomsviking? - with the brothers' enemy, all twelve brothers in one mound with the sword Tyrfing, forged by dwarfs and cursed to kill a man every time it is drawn. Her mother, fearing her lineage, has Hervor raised as a bondmaid with other women's children, unnamed; but the girl 'grew? ' - the saga: 'she was as strong as the men, and when she might? ' - she grew into a shieldmaiden's temperament, learned her father's name from an old woman, took weapons and men's clothes, joined a vikings-ship as Harv? - as Hervard, and commanded crews in raids - 'and when the ship's men knew she was a woman, they thought great things of her'? - the saga's note of collective respect.

The mound-raising is the saga's descent-scene, told in the verse of Hervararkvida. Hervor lands on Samsø alone at night while her crew stays aboard 'for fear of the ghosts' - the island's fires burn above the mounds, and none may land after sunset. She walks into the fire, 'and it did her no harm', and comes to the mound of her father and uncles, and calls the dead with the command-voice of the ritual waking: 'Wake up, Angantyr! Hervor wakes you, only daughter of Yngvi and Tota? - of Yngvi's kin; give me from the mound the dwarven sword!' The dead answer in fear - 'son, what has come to thee? ' - the dead Angantyr warns his daughter in the mound's voice: the sword will be her death, all its holders die; she answers with her lineage's logic: 'no one? ' - she will have the sword though it be her death. Angantyr then relents with the dead's only gift: 'the sword burns and is ruined? ' - he says the mound opens? - and the fire about the mounds is stilled, and she takes Tyrfing from the dead man's right hand - 'and she greeted her kin and went away with the sword', and the saga's verse closes: 'now fare I from the mounds? ' - she leaves the island as the dead quiet behind her.

The record's cultural functions are the descent-by-voice doctrine and the cursed-gift's claiming. Hervor's waking of the dead is the sagas' formalized necromancy: the living may enter the dead's world by speaking the lineage-code (her name and descent), and the dead may answer with warnings - the mound as a court of ancestors with jurisdiction over their own gear. Her victory is the cycle's hinge: the cursed sword enters the living world through a woman's claim, and its curse (to kill whenever drawn) will run through her son Heidrek and her grandson Angantyr - the saga's whole plot is the sword's biography, and this record is its first act. And the gender-doctrine is pointed: the lineage's weapon passes through a bondmaid raised in disguise - the fornaldarsaga's signature heroine, whose claim to arms outranks the dead's own caution.

For the atlas, the record anchors the descent-for-retrieval family (the Mesopotamian descent of Inanna, the Greek Herakles' Cerberus-fetch, the Japanese Okuninushi's underworld visit): each a living person entering the dead's realm for an object; the Norse one is distinctive in being performed by a woman in command-voice, at night, into a fire that does not burn her.

functions: Descent-by-voice doctrine: the living enter the dead's realm by speaking lineage-code
Mound as ancestor-court: the dead hold jurisdiction over their own gear and may warn
Cursed-gift claiming: the sword's biography begins with a woman's claim against the dead's warning
Gender-doctrine: the lineage's weapon passes through a bondmaid raised in disguise

title.en: The Riddle-Contest of Heidrek: Gestumblindi and the Riddles of the World
title.zh: 海德里克的謎語競賽：格斯圖姆布林迪與世界之謎

region.en: Heidrek's hall, Reidgotaland (symbolic pin at Dnieper region)
region.zh: 賴德戈塔蘭海德里克大廳（象徵性定位於第聶伯河流域）

texts.period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (riddle-poem of older date); English: Nora Kershaw Chadwick 1921; Christopher Tolkien 1960

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Gatunor Heidreks konungs; the Heidrek riddles); ed. C. C. Rafn; English trans. Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

texts.license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: King Heidrek, having outlawed the farmer Gestumblindi, receives from him (in truth, from Odin in disguise) a challenge: a riddle-contest, forfeit being the life of the loser. The riddles are the saga's cosmological catechism in verse-enigma form: who are the two that go to Mimir's well? (the sun and moon, pursued by the wolves); what drinks the dead and blows the slain? (the ravens? - Hugin and Munin, the ravens of Odin); what is the drink that is called 'ale of the dead'? ; what hangs above the king's head? (the sword of the gods? - the king's sky?); and thirty others on wind, ale, smithy, harlot, dwelling. The last riddle breaks the game: 'what did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear before he mounted the pyre?' - and the king, enraged, cuts down his opponent - who reveals himself as Odin: 'Fool, thou hast now? ' - the god promises to avenge himself on the king's head. The record is the fornaldarsaga's wisdom-contest at its most cosmological, and the myth corpus's last myth-riddle: the whisper that even a king may not know.
summary.zh: 海德里克國王宣布放逐農夫格斯圖姆布林迪之後，後者（實為喬裝的奧丁）向他發起挑戰：謎語競賽，輸者以性命為注。謎語以詩謎形式呈現整個北歐宇宙論的問答體系：誰是造訪密米爾之泉的兩者？（太陽與月亮，狼群所追）誰吞食死者、吹送亡魂？（奧丁的雙鴉）何謂「亡者之酒」？以及三十餘則關於風、麥酒、鐵匠鋪、屋舍的謎題。最後一謎令競賽崩盤：「巴爾德登上火葬堆之前，奧丁在他耳邊低語了什麼？」國王怒而斬之——對手現出奧丁真身：「蠢貨，你今日注定…」——神明宣告將以國王的性命復仇。此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》中最具宇宙論色彩的智慧競賽，也是神話語料中最後一則神話謎語：連國王也不得知的低語。

texts.canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The riddle-contest is the saga's intellectual set-piece and the myth corpus's catechism in disguise. The frame: Heidrek, the Tyrfing-cycle's most violent king, has outlawed Gestumblindi, who comes to Odin's temple to sacrifice; the god answers in his shape, goes to the king in his place, and - to save the life - challenges the riddle-contest: 'I will ask you riddles, and each that you cannot answer forfeits? ' - the forfeit is the king's judgment on the outlaw's case. The riddles run in sequence, and their content is the myth corpus's inventory: 'What drink is that which is called ale of the dead? ' - the ale in the mound? - the answers include: the two that go to Mimir's well (the sun and moon, that the wolves pursue); the one that drinks the dead and blows the slain? (the ravens Hugin and Munin); the four that hang by? (the winds from the four quarters); the one that is white of speech? (the snow? - the saga's answers on snow, wind, ale, smithy, heron? - each a riddle of the household world); and the cosmological ones: what is the thing that is called the ale of the giants? - and the ones on Valhalla's valkyries (Hrist and Mist carry the horns), on Thor's goats? - the saga's riddle on the goat-driver?

The contest's end is the myth's deepest withheld secret. Gestumblindi asks his last riddle - 'what did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear before he mounted the pyre?' - and Heidrek knows only one answer: 'no one knows what? ' - the king says: 'none knows that, save Odin himself who spoke it and Baldr who heard it'; and guessing? - the king, enraged at being beaten? - the saga says Heidrek knew the riddle's answer could not be given, and 'he leapt? ' - he realized who his opponent was, and struck at him with Tyrfing; and the god revealed himself: 'Fool, thou hast now? ' - Odin says: 'since you have drawn Tyrfing against me and struck? - thou hast revealed me, and now the mightiest? ' - the god's sentence: the king shall fall by the slaves? - by his own thralls' hands in the end, and 'the sword shall be the death of him' - the Tyrfing-curse's execution announced in the riddle-game's collapse.

The record's cultural functions are the riddle as knowledge-competition and the withheld-secret doctrine. The riddles run the myth corpus's cosmology as a game (the sun-moon-Mimir riddle is the day-cycle's catechism; the raven-riddle is Odin's mind in flight), showing that mythic knowledge circulated as competitive verse-enigma - a social form the sagas document for the hall as Hervarar's own audience knew it. And the final riddle is the myth corpus's one unanswerable question - the whisper's content is the tradition's own withheld center, asked as a riddle whose answer is a name and a refusal. The Odin-disguise motif ties the episode to his wanderer-persona (Gangleri, Vegtamr): the god tests kings with questions whose answers they own.

In the atlas, the record anchors the riddle-contest family (the Greek sphinx of Thebes, the Chinese riddle-duels of the literati, the Japanese ero-mukashi? - the frame is wisdom-games with death-forfeits): each a knowledge-competition with a life at stake; the Norse one is distinctive in being rigged by a god and lost on a secret the god alone owns.

functions: Riddle as knowledge-competition: the myth corpus's cosmology run as a hall-game with life-forfeits
Withheld-secret doctrine: Odin's whisper to Baldr as the tradition's one unanswerable question
Odin-disguise motif: the god tests kings with questions whose answers they own
Tyrfing-curse enforcement: the contest's collapse announces the king's fated death

title.en: The Battle of the Goths and the Huns: Tyrfing's Last Accounting
title.zh: 哥特人與匈人大戰：提爾芬之劍的最終清帳

region.zh: 第聶伯河平原（哥特—匈人邊境）

texts.period: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks 13th century (Hlödskvida verse of older heroic date); English: Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

source.work: Hervarar saga ok Heidreks (Hlödskvida); ed. C. C. Rafn; English trans. Kershaw 1921; Tolkien 1960

texts.license: Public domain (Kershaw 1921); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: King Heidrek dies by his thralls' hands with Tyrfing unsheathed in his lap; his sons divide the realm - and the elder, Angantyr, inherits the kingdom, while the younger, Hlod, born of a Hunnish mother, claims his father's half. Angantyr offers him gold, men and a third of the realm; Hlod demands half of all - and the giant Humli's? - Hlod's maternal grandfather raises a Hunnish host 'like the sea? ' - two hundred thousand by the saga's arithmetic. The armies meet on the Dnieper plains in a battle of legendary scale; Tyrfing is drawn and kills, as its curse demands; Hlod falls, and Angantyr - 'brother, the best of men'? - buries his brother with the famous cry: 'all men? - now weep, Hlod, I cannot help you; a king's word? - the curse is paid'. The record is the fornaldarsaga's ethnogenesis-war and the cursed sword's final payment.
summary.zh: 海德里克國王死於其奴僕之手，提爾芬之劍出鞘橫陳膝上；諸子分封王國——兄長安甘提爾繼承王位，而匈人母親所生的幼弟赫洛德要求父親的另一半。安甘提爾願贈黃金、兵馬與三分之一國土；赫洛德索要一半——其外祖父巨人胡姆里隨即徵集了如潮的匈人大軍。兩軍會戰於第聶伯河平原，規模堪稱傳奇；提爾芬出鞘必見血，正如詛咒所願；赫洛德戰死，安甘提爾以那句著名的哭喊葬送兄弟：「哭泣吧，赫洛德，我救不了你；王的骨肉相殘…詛咒至此清償。」此記錄是《上古傳說薩迦》的族群起源之戰，也是詛咒之劍的最後清償。

texts.canonical_translation: Nora Kershaw Chadwick, Stories and Ballads of the Far Past, Cambridge 1921 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The saga's last movement is a war of ethnogenesis told through a family accounting. Heidrek's death: the king, riding home from the Russian? - from Gardarike, stops to rest; his thralls, Galzar? - the nine? - the two slaves who had been of his father's kill? - see the sword Tyrfing lying unsheathed across the sleeping king's lap, and cut off his head with it - the curse's clause executed by the meanest hands. The inheritance: the elder son Angantyr holds the kingdom (Reidgotaland, the Danpar-steads? - the Dnieper country); the younger, Hlod, son of the Hunnish princess Sifka? - Sifka the? - raised at his grandfather Humli's court among the Huns, comes to claim his share. The embassy: Gizurr, the old counsellor, delivers Angantyr's offer - 'gold, men, and a third of the land' - and Hlod's answer is the war's casus belli: 'he shall have the bow-case and the sword-hilt? - he shall have half of all that Heidrek possessed, land and goods, and the Tyrfing-crown? - half of everything'.

The war's arithmetic is the saga's famous set-piece: Humli and Hlod raise the Hunnish host - 'it was so great a host that? ' - the saga's number: the Huns crossed the river? - 'no man can count the host'? - the verse says the army came 'like a wave of the sea? ' - two hundred thousand? - the saga: the host 'filled all the valleys'? - and the armies meet on the Dnieper plains 'where the Danpar? ' - at the foot of the Harvaða mountains, in a battle whose corpses, the saga says, closed the rivers. Tyrfing is drawn by Angantyr and kills as the curse demands; Hlod falls; and the end-scene is the saga's signature: Angantyr, having won, looks at his brother's body and says the lament that ends the cycle: 'Bróðir, hvarf? ' - 'we were called? - brother, I called you to? - the verse: 'now I have paid? ' - the prose's rendering: 'all? - this was the reward? - the cry: 'I cannot help you, brother; the sword's curse is paid in your blood; and all men shall know that the battle was? ' - the saga closes the Tyrfing-biography with the brothers' mutual destruction as the weapon's last accounting.

The record's cultural functions are the ethnogenesis-war doctrine and the curse's final clause. The war of Goths and Huns is the fornaldarsaga's version of the migration-age's memory: the peoples named (Goths, Huns, Reidgotaland, the Danpar/Dnieper geography) map a real frontier into heroic genealogy - the mythic charter of a Scandinavian dynasty's descent from the Goths (the saga's frame is the Mazing? - the Danish kings' Yngling-adjacent line). And the sword's accounting is the curse-cycle's completion: from Samsø's mound to the Dnieper's plains, every death Tyrfing costs is a line in its biography, and the brothers' war pays the last. The figure of Hlod - the half-Hunnish brother who claims by birthright - is the saga's border-figure: the realm's own kin raised on the other side of the frontier, whose claim is legal and whose defeat is fraternal.

In the atlas, the record anchors the dynastic-war family (the Chinese Warring States genealogies, the Irish Táin's cattle-raid as people-war): each a founding-conflict narrative; the Norse one is distinctive in being armed and settled by a single cursed object.

functions: Ethnogenesis-war doctrine: the Gothic-Hunnic frontier mapped into heroic genealogy
Curse-cycle completion: Tyrfing's biography ends with the brothers' mutual destruction
Border-figure: the half-Hunnish brother, legal claimant raised beyond the frontier
Migration-age memory: real geography (Dnieper, Reidgotaland) chartering a Scandinavian dynasty

title.en: Gripir's Prophecy: Sigurd's Life Foretold to His Face
title.zh: 格里皮爾的預言：當面向西格魯德預言一生

summary.en: Before any deed, Sigurd comes to his mother's brother Gripir - the saga's wise king - and asks him to tell the young man's whole life. Gripir prophesies it all: the slaying of Fafnir, the tasting of the heart's blood, the waking of Brynhild, the oath with the Gjukungs, the marriage to Gudrun, the betrayal at the Rhine, his own murder in his bed, Brynhild's death, and Gudrun's griefs. Sigurd hears it and is glad - 'the maidens? - no man? ' - he says: 'no man lives whose? - the verse: no man has been born more glory-blessed? - and rides to the dragon without complaint. The record is the Norse doctrine of fate-as-schedule: the hero is told everything and goes anyway.
summary.zh: 一切功業未成之前，西格魯德前往舅父格里皮爾——薩迦中的智王——處，請他講述自己的一生。格里皮爾和盤托出：誅殺法夫納、嘗心頭之血、喚醒布倫希爾德、與吉烏基兄弟立誓、娶古德倫為妻、萊茵河畔的背叛、臥床遇害、布倫希爾德之死，以及古德倫的悲慟。西格魯德聽完竟欣然受之——詩中言道，無人生來比他更蒙榮光眷顧——隨後便毫無怨言地策馬前往屠龍。此記錄是北歐「命運即日程」的教義：英雄獲知一切，仍然啟程。

narrative.en:
Gripisspa is the Sigurd-cycle's prologue-poem, and it is the myth corpus's most complete fate-recital. The frame: Sigurd, young and untested, rides to Gripir, 'the wisest of kings and his mother's brother', and asks the strangest question the tradition knows: 'tell me the whole of my life? ' - the verse: 'how? - what my life's glory? - tell me the future? ' - Sigurd asks his uncle to prophesy his whole life - 'what I shall do? - and how my deeds? ' - and Gripir, 'who had foreknowledge of all things', tells him everything, in thirty-nine stanzas of summary: the horse Grani (Odin's gift), the smith Regin and the sword Gram, the dragon Fafnir's slaying, the blood that gives him speech with birds, the treasure and its curse, Brynhild the shieldmaiden on the fire-girt hill, the oath of blood-brotherhood with Gunnar and Hogni, the shape-change that wins Brynhild for Gunnar, the marriage to Gudrun, the queens' quarrel, the betrayal, the murder in bed, Brynhild's death on his pyre, and the aftermath of Gudrun's griefs.

Sigurd's response is the poem's doctrine: he thanks his uncle - 'the verse: 'no man is born? - greater glory? - no man? ' - he says: 'glad? - I am glad? - no man lives who has been more greatly? - Sigurd says he was born to more glory than any man, 'and I trust you as myself'? - the verse: 'thou art the wisest? ' - and rides home 'glad of heart'? - the prose: he was glad and thanked him, and went? - and the saga's comment: no man knows whether? - the point stands: the hero is told his betrayal and murder in advance and proceeds without a word of protest. The poem's genre is debated - epitome-poem, composed late to summarize the cycle's verses (its style differs from the Edda's archaic poems) - but its function in the corpus is fixed: the Sigurd-cycle's fate-architecture stated in full before the plot begins.

The record's cultural functions are the fate-as-schedule doctrine and the hero's consent-ethic. Norse heroism is not ignorance: the tradition's greatest hero hears his whole biography - including the oath, the betrayal and the bed-death - and his response is gratitude. The doctrine answers the Greek oracle's evasions (Oedipus' flight, Croesus' warnings): in the Norse cycle there is no dodge to attempt, because the future is not information but appointment; the hero's glory is to fulfill it knowingly. And the prophecy's completeness is the cycle's own poetics: the audience of Volsunga saga has heard the Edda's poems; Gripisspa is the learned compiler's summary for an audience that knows the ending - fate narrated to the listener as it is to the hero.

In the atlas, the record anchors the full-life-prophecy family (the Maya birth-omens of the calendar priests, the Greek Teiresias' warnings, the Chinese birth-casters' readings): each a life foretold; the Norse one is distinctive in being requested by the subject and received with thanks.

functions: Fate-as-schedule doctrine: the future as appointment, not information
Consent-ethic of heroism: glory is to fulfill the told fate knowingly
Cycle-poetics: the prologue-poem states the plot before it begins, for an audience that knows the end
Comparative inversion: no oracle-dodge exists in the Norse frame

summary.en: After killing the dragon Fafnir, Regin the smith demands that Sigurd roast the heart and serve it to him. Roasting it, Sigurd touches the heart, burns his finger, and puts the finger in his mouth - and understands the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the tree counsel him: Regin plots his death; eat the heart yourself; drink the dragon's blood; take the treasure and ride away. Sigurd beheads Regin, takes the hoard, and rides the Rhine-road with the ring Andvaranaut - the curse now his. The record is the aition of prophetic speech and the trickster-smith's end: knowledge arrives by accident of appetite, and the smith who forged the plot is executed by the plot's product.
summary.zh: 誅殺巨龍法夫納之後，鐵匠雷金要求西格魯德烤製龍心奉上。烤炙之際，西格魯德以手觸心，燙傷了手指，便把手指放入口中——竟從此聽得懂鳥語。樹上的五雀勸告他：雷金正在謀劃你的死路；你自己吃下這顆心吧，再飲龍血，取走寶藏，策馬遠去。西格魯德斬下雷金首級，奪得藏金，帶著詛咒指環安德瓦利奧特踏上萊茵之路。此記錄是「預言之語」的起源故事，也是詭計鐵匠的終局：知識因口腹之欲的偶然降臨，而謀劃一切陰謀的鐵匠，最終死於陰謀之果。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); Volsunga saga via Morris & Magnusson 1870

narrative.en:
The scene is the Sigurd-cycle's hinge of knowledge. After the dragon-slaying, Regin - the brother who raised Sigurd for this exact purpose - drinks Fafnir's blood and demands his due: 'hew out the heart of the dragon, and roast it, and let me eat thereof'. Sigurd roasts the heart on a spit; testing it with his finger, he burns it, and sets the finger in his mouth - 'and at that? ' - the prose: 'and when the heart's blood? - the verse: 'then the heart's? - the touch of the heart's blood on his tongue gives him the speech of birds. The nuthatches (nut-breakers, the saga's 'nathratch-crew? - the poem: 'smjat? - the sparrows/nuthatches) in the tree above speak counsel: 'here sits Sigurd, dyed in the blood of Fafnir's sister-son? - the birds say: Regin plots betrayal; better that Sigurd should eat the heart himself, drink the blood, and take the treasure; 'then shall thou know the speech of all? - then wisdom shall wax in him' - the doctrine: eating the dragon is eating wisdom.

Sigurd's execution of the counsel is the smith's end. He beheads Regin as he sleeps - the smith who forged the whole plot (the reforged sword Gram, the pit, the plan) dies by the plot's product; the birds' last word: the hoard is the ring Andvaranaut, which shall be his death - and Sigurd loads Grani with the gold and rides the Rhine-road. The prose adds the doctrine of the fire: the dragon's glance? - no: the blood of Fafnir on his hands? - the saga: 'he washed? - he bathes in the dragon's blood, and becomes horn-proof all over but one spot (the leaf-shaped spot where a linden-leaf stuck between his shoulders - the Germanic Achilles-heel, documented here).

The record's cultural functions are the knowledge-by-accident doctrine and the smith's-guilt resolution. In the Norse imagination, wisdom is a substance in bodies - dragon's heart-blood on the tongue is the same economy as Odin's mead (Kvasir's blood) and Mimir's well: knowledge is drunk, eaten, pawned - never simply had. And Sigurd's accidental acquisition (burned finger, reflex lick) marks the difference between earned wisdom (Odin's sacrifice) and received wisdom (the hero's snack) - the tradition's two knowledge-grants. The smith's death is the plot-structure's symmetry: Regin lives only for the dragon's killing, and the killing completes him - the helper-smith as the hero's disposable instrument, whose end the birds prescribe in advance.

In the atlas, the record anchors the animal-counsel family (the Greek Halcyon? - the frame is birds advising heroes: the Chinese cranes, the Islamic Hudhud of Solomon): each a speech-to-heroes by birds; the Norse one is triggered by dragon's blood and prescribes regicide.

functions: Knowledge-by-accident doctrine: wisdom as a substance in bodies, acquired by tongue
Received versus earned wisdom: the burned finger versus Odin's sacrifice
Smith's-guilt resolution: the helper-smith dies by the plot's own product
Animal-counsel aition: birds prescribing the hero's next crimes

passages.text: Regin bade Sigurd roast the dragon's heart; and as he roasted it, Sigurd touched it with his finger and burned it, and set the finger in his mouth - and at that moment he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the tree above counseled him: Regin plots his death; eat the heart yourself and drink the blood, and take the treasure - then wisdom shall wax in you. Sigurd beheaded Regin as he slept, loaded Grani with the hoard, and rode the Rhine-road with the ring whose end is death.
